title: AI-Assisted Microbiome Analysis
text:
Practice with synthetic data
Follow one workflow from checked input tables to figures you can explain: practise, explore supplied datasets, then analyse your own data.
You will work from prepared feature tables. Raw sequencing processing and statistical hypothesis testing are outside this guide’s workflow.
Begin with 24 synthetic samples and 15 fictional features. Learn to read composition and Shannon diversity plots, then check the figures against the saved tables. An optional exercise reproduces one sample’s values.
Begin the practice example

title: AI-Assisted Microbiome Analysis
text:
Follow the DietSwap walkthrough
Use the supplied study tables to investigate composition and diversity. Check the participant and sampling information before deciding which comparison the data support.
Follow the DietSwap walkthrough

title: AI-Assisted Microbiome Analysis
text:
Apply the workflow to Mouse59
Explore 59 samples and 2,027 OTUs in two supplied groups. Compare OTU composition and diversity, investigate low-count samples, and verify your observations against the tables.
This demonstration uses OTU identifiers as labels because taxonomic assignments are unavailable.
Follow the Mouse59 demonstration

title: AI-Assisted Microbiome Analysis
text:
Analyse your own study
Prepare your three tidy TSV files in data/my-study/, check the identifiers, and apply the same workflow. Verify the results and write a conclusion supported by your evidence.
Prepare your own analysis
Use Run the workflow whenever a page asks you to generate or refresh outputs.

title: Set up your workspace
text:
Before you begin
Complete this setup before beginning the guide. You will download the project files, open your workspace, and restore the R packages needed for all three examples.
Work through the sections in order. You only need to complete this setup once.
Have R, Quarto, and an editor such as VS Code or RStudio installed on your computer.

title: Set up your workspace
text:
Get the project files
Download the project ZIP

Extract the downloaded ZIP.
Open the extracted ai-assisted-microbiome-analysis-main folder in VS Code or RStudio.
Open a terminal in that folder.







Note



This is your project folder, also called the repository root. It contains _quarto.yml, renv.lock, data/, scripts/, and templates/. Run the guide’s terminal commands from this folder.

title: Set up your workspace
text:
Restore the R environment
The project includes renv.lock, which records the R packages used for the supplied analyses.






Where does code run?



Run terminal commands such as R, Rscript, and quarto in your terminal. After starting R, run R expressions at the R prompt (>). Opening a guide page does not run its code.


In the terminal, start R:
R
At the R prompt (>), run:
options(repos = c(CRAN = "https://cloud.r-project.org"))

if (!requireNamespace("renv", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("renv")
}

renv::restore()
renv::status()
If asked to proceed, enter Y and wait for the > prompt before entering another command. Restore the supplied lockfile rather than initializing a new environment.
Check that the analysis packages load, then return to the terminal:
library(tidyverse)
library(vegan)

q(save = "no")






Note



If setup fails: copy the error message. Ask AI to explain it using your R version, operating system, and the command you ran. Check the proposed fix before applying it. Keep the supplied lockfile intact while investigating.

title: Begin the synthetic practice
text:
How to follow along
Question: How do community composition and diversity vary between two groups?
Use 24 synthetic samples, 12 per group, and 15 fictional features to learn the workflow. You will produce three figures, inspect the tables, and write a short explanation.
Complete workspace setup once before running commands.
Next: Preview the practice figures

title: Begin the synthetic practice
text:
Preview the supplied figures to see what you will produce.
Meet the three input files and check their identifiers.
Run the practice analysis using the shared command page.
Compare your figures with the tables and write your explanation.







Note



The figures describe this teaching dataset. Your task is to explain the visible patterns and check the numbers. An optional sample calculation is available if you want to inspect how Shannon diversity is obtained.

title: Read the practice figures
text:
Preview the supplied results first. You will reproduce them after checking the inputs; you do not need to run anything to read this page.



Composition of the synthetic samples.


Each bar sums to 100%. Compare the same feature across samples. Other pools seven features, so inspect the unpooled table before attributing its difference to any one feature.



Shannon diversity in the synthetic samples.


Each point is one sample. Compare the medians, spread, and overlap, then check the numerical values in the diversity table.



Count totals and Shannon diversity in the synthetic samples.


Look for a relationship within each group. Record whether the count ranges overlap before explaining the diversity difference.

text:

Measure
Expected value

6006

For each feature, divide its count by the sample total to obtain its proportion. Calculate \(H=-\sum p_i\ln(p_i)\) using positive proportions.
The synthetic table gives median Shannon diversity of about 2.428 in Group A and 2.560 in Group B. All samples have 15 observed features, so this diversity difference reflects evenness in the supplied proportions.

title: Follow the DietSwap study
text:
Question. How do community composition and diversity compare between the cohorts in the selected DietSwap samples?
The supplied DietSwap tables in data/dietswap/ contain 38 samples from 38 distinct participants, with 21 AAM and 17 AFR samples. They include 119 features.
All supplied samples have timepoint = 1, timepoint.within.group = 1, and study_group = ED. This walkthrough compares the selected cohorts at that sampling stage. Confirm its baseline meaning against the source documentation when reporting the study.
Next: Define the comparison

title: Define the comparison
text:
Open the metadata and write one sentence naming the cohorts, sampling stage, and unit of analysis. Count unique participants as well as samples.
The supplied selection contains one sample per participant. Compare the cohorts at the supplied sampling stage. Calling this a baseline comparison requires documentation of what the time-point labels mean.
After your run, return to the figures linked on the verification page. Record one observation before writing an explanation.
Next: Meet the study files

title: Meet the DietSwap files
text:
Check the supplied selection
Use the same three filenames and columns as the practice dataset, stored in data/dietswap/. Preserve the participant, nationality, sampling stage, and time-point columns in the metadata.
Set group to the intended comparison and record how it was defined. Check the source study and data documentation before choosing a baseline label or interpreting a field. Record the source, selection rule, sample count, and exclusions.
The metadata use AAM and AFR for both nationality and the comparison group. There is one sample per subject. All 38 records have the same supplied sampling labels (time point 1, within-group time point 1, ED). The 119 feature IDs match taxonomy exactly.
The taxonomy table contains rank labels that need review against the source annotation before reporting a particular taxonomic rank.
Next: Check the selection

title: Check the DietSwap selection
text:
Confirm that sample IDs match the count table, feature IDs match taxonomy, and the selected samples answer the question. Review repeated participant IDs and missing group labels.
Use the DietSwap command. Its automatic checks validate the table structure. Confirm the participant and time-point selection yourself.






Two kinds of checks



The script checks file structure and matching IDs. You check whether the selected participants and sampling stage support your question.


Next: Inspect the outputs

text:
Open results/dietswap/tables/alpha-diversity.tsv after the run. Reconcile its sample count and group labels with your selected metadata.
Inspect all three figures and locate the table behind each. Record the sample with the lowest and highest Shannon values and check its count total and observed richness.

Describe the count ranges and any visible relationship with Shannon within each cohort.
Write a conclusion restricted to the selected samples and sampling stage. A comparison at one sampling stage does not estimate change after a diet swap.

title: Apply the workflow to Mouse59
text:
You have practised with synthetic data and followed the DietSwap walkthrough. Now apply the same workflow to a larger OTU table.
Question: How do OTU composition, Shannon diversity, and feature-table count totals differ between samples labelled HighFat20 and HighFatCa?
This demonstration contains 59 samples and 2,027 OTUs. Keep the supplied group names throughout. The exercise describes patterns in these files; detailed study context is unavailable. Taxonomic assignments are unavailable, so figures display OTU identifiers.
By the end, you will check the inputs, reproduce the figures, check the tables, and write a conclusion supported by numerical evidence.
Use data/mouse59/ for the supplied inputs and results/mouse59/ for outputs. Keep data/my-study/ for your own study.
Next: See the results
crumbs: 18  Apply the workflow to Mouse59

title: See the Mouse59 results
text:
OTU composition
The figures below show the supplied results. Preview them now; you will use the shared workflow instructions to reproduce them after checking the inputs.
OTU0440 generally occupies a larger proportion in HighFat20. HighFatCa has variable contributions from other displayed OTUs, and many samples have a larger pooled Other fraction. Other represents many OTUs, not one organism. Every bar sums to 100%, regardless of the original count total.
Open the composition figure at full size to read the sample IDs and legend.

title: See the Mouse59 results
text: Relative proportions of the eight OTUs with the highest mean sample proportions; all remaining OTUs are pooled as Other. Each bar is one sample.

title: See the Mouse59 results
text:
Shannon diversity



Shannon diversity calculated using all 2,027 OTUs, using positive proportions in the Shannon formula. Each point is one sample.


The median Shannon value is higher in HighFatCa: 3.595117, compared with 2.811773 in HighFat20. The distributions overlap. Shannon reflects both the number of observed OTUs and how evenly counts are distributed among them; higher values do not establish a healthier community.

title: See the Mouse59 results
text:
Count totals and diversity



Feature-table count totals and Shannon diversity for each Mouse59 sample.


Samples with similar count totals can have different Shannon values. Two samples have especially small totals, 99 and 182. The sample with the lowest Shannon value has a much larger total, so low counts alone do not explain every low diversity value. This scatterplot does not establish that count depth has no influence.
These observations describe the supplied data. The workflow does not test statistical significance or establish a treatment effect.
Next: Meet the inputs

title: Meet the Mouse59 inputs
text:
The original Mouse59GutOTUs.csv contained samples in rows, a Class column, and OTUs in columns. Preparation transposed the count table and retained the original counts and labels.







File in data/mouse59/
Contents




feature-counts.tsv
feature_id, followed by 59 sample columns; 2,027 OTU rows


sample-metadata.tsv
sample_id and group; 29 HighFat20 and 30 HighFatCa samples


taxonomy.tsv
feature_id, an OTU ID in taxon, and a note marking the assignment as unavailable



The taxonomy file supplies display labels required by the workflow. It contains no biological taxonomic assignments. Describe the composition figure in terms of OTUs.
All samples have positive totals. Counts range from 99 to 40,266 per sample, with an overall median of 22,150. No OTU has a zero total across all samples. No filtering, normalization, or rarefaction was applied during input preparation.
Do not infer the meaning of HighFat20 or HighFatCa from their names. For this exercise, treat them as supplied sample categories. Animal identity, cage membership, repeated sampling, and other covariates are unavailable in these inputs.






What is an OTU?



An operational taxonomic unit is a sequence-based feature. Here, OTU IDs are the available labels; they do not identify named species.


Next: Check the inputs

title: Check the Mouse59 inputs
text:
Confirm that all three TSV files are in data/mouse59/. Follow the shared workflow instructions, using the Mouse59 input and output folders.
The analysis script checks the inputs before calculating results. Resolve any error before interpreting outputs.
Check that:

There are 59 unique sample IDs, matching exactly between counts and metadata.
There are 2,027 unique feature IDs, matching the taxonomy display-label file.
Counts are finite, nonnegative integers and every sample has a positive total.
Group sizes are HighFat20 = 29 and HighFatCa = 30.

A valid file format does not guarantee adequate data for every question. Both low-count samples pass the positive-total requirement. Record SRR4125132 (99 counts) and SRR4125107 (182 counts) for further investigation.
Keep all 59 samples in the initial demonstration. Any later exclusion should have a stated rationale and a separate output folder so you can compare results.






A useful quality check



A nonzero total passes the structural check, but a very small total may give an incomplete view of the community. Record the two low-count samples before deciding whether a sensitivity analysis is useful.


Next: Inspect the outputs

title: Inspect the Mouse59 outputs
text:
Use the Mouse59 command on the Run the workflow page. If you have already generated these results, continue with the checks below.
Open results/mouse59/tables/alpha-diversity.tsv. Confirm it contains one row for each of the 59 samples and the expected group labels.
Locate the three figures in results/mouse59/figures/:

composition.png
shannon-diversity.png
depth-diversity.png

Use the saved tables to answer these questions:

Which sample has the lowest Shannon value? What are its total counts and observed OTUs?
Which sample has the highest Shannon value?
Do the group medians agree with the values on the results page?
Does OTU0440 have a higher mean sample proportion in HighFat20? Calculate its relative proportion within each sample before averaging by group.

Use tables/relative-abundance.tsv to check composition. The display table groups features for plotting; Shannon uses the full feature table. Do not calculate Shannon from the eight displayed OTUs plus Other.

title: Verify and explain Mouse59
text:
Explain what the checks mean
A matching Shannon value confirms the calculation for that sample. It does not establish that the sample has adequate coverage or that a group difference has a biological cause. For example, a sample with only 99 counts can still have a relatively high Shannon value if those counts are spread across many OTUs.
Return to the three figures. Write one observation per figure and support each with a table value. Separate what you observed from possible explanations.
An appropriate diversity statement is:

In the supplied Mouse59 table, HighFatCa samples had a higher median Shannon diversity than HighFat20 samples (3.595117 versus 2.811773), with overlapping values between groups. This descriptive comparison does not establish statistical significance or explain the difference.

title: Verify and explain Mouse59
text:
Questions to carry forward

How sensitive are the patterns to the two low-count samples?
Does observed richness show the same pattern as Shannon?
Which individual OTUs contribute to the pooled Other fraction?
What additional metadata would be needed to account for animals, cages, or repeated samples?

Do not choose exclusions or analysis methods solely because they strengthen a preferred group difference.

title: Appendix A — Workflow reference
text:
Terms used in the figures
The R workflow starts from integer feature counts, sample metadata, and supplied taxonomic labels. Shannon uses natural logarithms and all original features. Top-eight selection and Other apply to the composition display.
The supplied scripts produce descriptive summaries. Study design, pairing, confounding, and statistical inference require decisions beyond these plots.
Use Run the workflow for commands and Write a report for the report template.
Zero proportions contribute zero to Shannon and are omitted from the logarithm calculation. The same displayed feature can change proportion when other features change; proportions alone do not measure absolute abundance.

title: Appendix A — Workflow reference
text:
Term
Meaning in this workflow




Feature
A row in the count table, such as an OTU or another supplied microbial feature


Count total
Sum of all feature counts in one sample; not a measure of total microbial biomass


Relative proportion
Feature count divided by that sample’s count total


Observed features
Number of features with a positive count in one sample


Shannon diversity
Summary of richness and evenness, using natural logarithms


Other
All features outside the top eight, pooled only for display
